subject: Outfiles listing diferentially methylated sites are empty

messages.author: 23a2cb256755f4e1
messages.subject: Outfiles listing diferentially methylated sites are empty
parts:
I understand that outfiles listing hypermethylated or Hypomethylated can be empty simply because there are not DMR between the compared samples. However I'm sure this is not the case and please let me explain before go to my question.

I have  4 samples ( control vs treatment with  2 replicates each). If I compare tiles of 100 bp with a step.size of 50 I get a bunch of DMR. However if I try to compare site by site instead of regions I got nothing. This do not have sense to me and I suspect I'm doing something wrong during the analysis. I willl appreciate if someone can read the commands i used and help me to identify my error.

#### Methyl seq sample detail
SAMPLE

C4_ctrl       BC1    REP1 control
C7_ctrl       BC5    REP2 control

C4_PEG    BC3    REP1 treatment
C7_PEG    BC7    REP2 treatment



### In this example I'm comparing  control=ctrl samples against the treatament=PEG in any context (CG, CHG, CHH) from; chr1
library(methylKit);
library(graphics);
comparisonName="C_ctrl_vs_C_PEG_anyContext_site_by_site";ou
chrom="chr1";
C4_ctrl="BC1"; C7_ctrl="BC5";
C4_PEG="BC3"; C7_PEG="BC7";
ctrl1=paste(C4_ctrl, chrom, "MethylKit.inputdata.anyContext.txt", sep=".");
ctrl2=paste(C7_ctrl, chrom, "MethylKit.inputdata.anyContext.txt", sep=".");
PEG1=paste(C4_PEG, chrom, "MethylKit.inputdata.anyContext.txt", sep=".");
PEG2=paste(C7_PEG, chrom, "MethylKit.inputdata.anyContext.txt", sep=".");
file.list <- list(ctrl1,ctrl2,PEG1,PEG2);
myobj <- read(file.list, sample.id = list(ctrl1,ctrl2,PEG1,PEG2), assembly="TAIR10", treatment=c(1,1,0,0), context="anyContext");
filtered.myobj=filterByCoverage(myobj,lo.count=10,lo.perc=NULL,hi.count=NULL,hi.perc=99.9)
meth <- unite(myobj, destrand = FALSE);
myDiff <- calculateDiffMeth(meth, num.cores=4);

#filtering for significant differential methylation
myDiff.hyper <- get.methylDiff(myDiff, difference = 10, qvalue = 0.01, type = "hyper");
myDiff.hypo <- get.methylDiff(myDiff, difference = 10, qvalue = 0.01, type = "hypo");

#output data for hypermethylated, hypomethylated, and all tiles
outfile1 = paste(comparisonName, chrom, "hyper", "txt", sep=".");
write.table(as.data.frame(myDiff.hyper), file=outfile1, sep="\t", col.names=TRUE, row.names=FALSE);
outfile2 = paste(comparisonName, chrom, "hypo", "txt", sep=".");
write.table(as.data.frame(myDiff.hypo), file=outfile2, sep="\t", col.names=TRUE, row.names=FALSE);
outfile3 = paste(comparisonName, chrom, "united", "txt", sep=".");
write.table(as.data.frame(meth), file=outfile3, sep="\t", col.names=TRUE, row.names=FALSE);

the result is that outfile 1 and outfile2 are empty.. What I did wrong?

I will appreciate any help

messages.author: ab8277113f65c05e
messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] Outfiles listing diferentially methylated sites are empty
parts:
I suggest take one of differentially methylated windows, find Cs overlapping with it, and do the differential methylation calculation per base for those regions. Check the percent methylation differences for those Cs, are they close to your cutoff ? Also see below

 I don't expect one to one correspondence between DMRs and DMCs. DMR calculation doesn't really depend on individual bases being differentially methylated, the number of methylated Cs and unmethylated Cs pooled over a region, that sort of pooling can cause differences in correspondence, where a DMR may not have DMCs. But main reason could be the following: in your DMRs there might be bases that are not covered in all samples, pooling counts per region will ignore whether or not each base covered in all samples or not. This is practical for sparsely covered genomes, because doing per base analysis will remove the bases from the analysis if they are not covered in all samples. By doing regional analysis you keep the information from the bases that are not covered in all samples.

Best,
Altuna

messages.author: e4181d5c40fc094c
messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] Outfiles listing diferentially methylated sites are empty
parts:
Altuna has pointed a very important issue in the analysis of methylation data. I would like to add one more point and I welcome further comments on this.

Performing 'regionscounts' on a methylRawList object may include the CpGs that are not covered in all the samples. From my point of view, this also leads to bias in calculation of the methylation status. To, expand this point consider this case. A 'promoter' of length 1.2kb may have 40 CpGs covered in sample1 (spread uniformly across the length) and sample2 with just 20 CpGs covered (on side of the promoter and not on other side). If we perform 'regioncounts' at this stage, we tend to calculate the methylation status from 40 CpGs of sample1 and just 20CpGs of sample2 which is biased due to under representation in sample2.

One possible way is to perform 'unite' function first and perform 'regioncounts' on the methylBase obj. This ensures that we consider only the common 20 CpGs in both samples. Some may find this option as conservative and wastage of methylation information in the data. But, my understanding is that in such a case we are more close to accuracy and comparison happens between CpGs of similar/dissimilar status at the same location. Additional CpGs (20 CpGs from Sample1) do add additional information and tweaks/neutralizes the methylations status of the region in their favour which are not represented in Sample2.


Regards,
Kalyan

parts:
Hi Altuna, thanks for your quick answer. Since I just start getting familiar with methylKit my first concern was that I was not doing the right sequence of commands or that I did not use the correct arguments in some of them. However according to your answer it looks like this was not the problem.

I'm following your suggestion but some of your explanation bring me concerns.

You said: "I don't expect one to one correspondence between DMRs and DMCs."

I was expecting that if one tile shows up as significantly differentially methylated, at least one cytosine must be differentially methylated.   But if I understand correctly you said that even though not single C in a tile is differentially methylated, the contribution of many not significant differences can produce a consolidated differentially methylated tile. I feel it kind of contra-intuitive but if possible do you think that my more that 1000 DMR found in chr1 showed up in this way?
Then you said that other reason could be lack of coverage. If I understand correctly you are saying that most of my DMR come out of regions that were poorly covered (and the many often one of the samples has not reads) or "bias ly" covered...may be 30 or 50 reads in 3 of the four libraries but one got zero.

Are both explanation indicating that is not god idea to perform calculateDiffMeth in a tiled genome?
Instead of filter by coverage in all, is there any way of filter by average??




"From Altuna"

I suggest take one of differentially methylated windows, find Cs overlapping with it, and do the differential methylation calculation per base for those regions. Check the percent methylation differences for those Cs, are they close to your cutoff ? Also see below

 I don't expect one to one correspondence between DMRs and DMCs. DMR calculation doesn't really depend on individual bases being differentially methylated, the number of methylated Cs and unmethylated Cs pooled over a region, that sort of pooling can cause differences in correspondence, where a DMR may not have DMCs. But main reason could be the following: in your DMRs there might be bases that are not covered in all samples, pooling counts per region will ignore whether or not each base covered in all samples or not. This is practical for sparsely covered genomes, because doing per base analysis will remove the bases from the analysis if they are not covered in all samples. By doing regional analysis you keep the information from the bases that are not covered in all samples.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] Outfiles listing diferentially methylated sites are empty
parts:
Kalyan
I agree with you. If you look at my original post you will find that after reading my files and filtering by coverage I united my samples. Just then I calculated DiffMeth. I think that the example that you bring is a highly likely  scenario (also highly dependent of coverage). Besides your suggestion I also think that using smaller tiles and shorter steps can avoid these kind of problems. For mouse and human and outside of CpG island you have one CpG every 110 bp (in average). may be a 250 bp tile will be more conservative than a 1000 bp one. In a future it will  be also nice if the package can tile and step in function of the CpG density.

Alejandro

parts: I was expecting that if one tile shows up as significantly differentially methylated, at least one cytosine must be differentially methylated.   But if I understand correctly you said that even though not single C in a tile is differentially methylated, the contribution of many not significant differences can produce a consolidated differentially methylated tile. I feel it kind of contra-intuitive but if possible do you think that my more that 1000 DMR found in chr1 showed up in this way?

This kind of effect could occur when pooling, DMRs and DMCs should not differ drastically if that is the sole reason. That's why I asked if the DMRs have borderline DMCs? I don't think 1000 DMRs can show up this way but it would be good to check if there are borderline DMCs in them. I also suggest that you don't use overlapping windows, this might  inflate the overall number of DMRs and not good for multiple testing correction. The correction assumes the tests are independent, if windows are overlapping tests are not independent.

Then you said that other reason could be lack of coverage. If I understand correctly you are saying that most of my DMR come out of regions that were poorly covered (and the many often one of the samples has not reads) or "bias ly" covered...may be 30 or 50 reads in 3 of the four libraries but one got zero.

I think this is more probable reason where you have non-uniform coverage over the bases. But if your tiles are small, you can get away with this. Literature suggest that CpGs (not sure this is true for all species I remember a publication about bees and we did something similar for human) close-by are correlated in their methylation levels. So if you take that into account, tilling on small windows could work and can interpolate methylation levels of regions even you don't have coverage over the bases.

Are both explanation indicating that is not god idea to perform calculateDiffMeth in a tiled genome?
Instead of filter by coverage in all, is there any way of filter by average??

I think tiling could work. You can try to show first spatial correlation between CpGs or Cs, if there is than you can tile and then unite(). If not, the only option is to first create a methylBase object containing bases then tile. This will remove bases that are not covered in all samples then you will be able to tile just using those bases
